title: Stacks Clarity: who actually called the contract
summary: Clarity separates tx-sender from contract-caller. Confusing them lets a hostile contract act with another user's privileges. We rebuild the authorization mistake and the post-condition habit that limits damage.

case.name: Clarity authorization class (tx-sender vs contract-caller)
case.impact: Class of bugs across early Stacks DeFi: privileged actions gated on the wrong principal

body:
Stacks smart contracts are written in Clarity, a decidable language that runs on the Stacks chain anchored to Bitcoin. Authorization in Clarity is not msg.sender from Ethereum. Two built-ins matter. tx-sender is the principal that originated the transaction. contract-caller is the principal that invoked the current contract in this call frame. When user A calls contract B and B calls contract C, inside C the contract-caller is B while tx-sender is still A.

Early Stacks apps sometimes gated admin or transfer functions with (is-eq tx-sender OWNER). That looks safe until a malicious contract is invited into the call path. If the check should mean "the immediate caller is the owner" but uses tx-sender, a contract called by the owner can escalate. The correct check depends on intent: user-initiated actions often want tx-sender; callbacks and vaults often want contract-caller or an explicit allowlist of contracts.

Clarity also has post-conditions: the wallet can require that asset movements in the transaction match an exact pattern. Post-conditions do not replace on-contract checks, but they bound what a confused deputy can steal in one transaction. They are part of Stacks' security culture the way associated token account checks are part of Solana's.

Compared with Solana's account model, Stacks still needs explicit principal checks. The bug class is confused deputy / wrong caller identity. ZKCTF's Solana program checks PDA identity before trusting vault data for the same reason: the caller chooses what you see until you prove who they are.

Reproduction exercise: read the Clarity snippet and name which built-in the code should use if only the immediate calling contract may mint.

exercise.statement: The mint function should allow only a specific vault contract to call it, not any transaction that the vault's owner happens to have signed earlier in a longer call chain. Which Clarity built-in should appear in the (is-eq … VAULT) check? Answer ZKCTF{built_in}.
artifacts:
(define-public (mint (amount uint))
  (begin
    ;; BUG: wrong principal for "immediate caller must be VAULT"
    (asserts! (is-eq tx-sender VAULT) (err u401))
    (ft-mint? token amount tx-sender)))
hints: tx-sender stays the original signer across inner contract calls.
The other built-in names the principal of the current call frame.
